The third opinion: it is Muḥammad (ﷺ), whom He taught the clarification of what has been and what will be; said by Ibn Kaysān.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾, that is, by calculation and stations, which they do not transgress. We have explained this meaning in [al-Anʿām: 96]. Al-Akhfash said: the predicate is omitted, and I think—and God knows best—that he meant: "they run by a reckoning."

(p-107) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾. Concerning "the star" there are two opinions. The first: it is every plant that has no stem; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, Muqātil, and the philologists. The second: it is the star of the sky, and by it is meant all the stars; said by Mujāhid. As for "the tree," it is everything that has a stem. al-Farrāʾ said: their prostration is that they face the sun when it rises, then they incline with it until the shade breaks. I have pointed out the meaning of the prostration of what does not understand in [al-Naḥl: 49]. Abū ʿUbayda said: their verb was dualized only according to their wording.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the heaven—He raised it﴾. He did this so that living beings would live and breaths would extend, and He sent the wind between it and the earth so that [creation] might be refreshed. Were it not so, creatures would have died of suffocation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions. The first: it is justice; said by the majority, among them Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and the philologists. al-Zajjāj said: this is because "al-muʿādala" is the weighing of things against each other. The second: it is the well-known balance, so that people may be equitable in rights; said by al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The third: it is the Qur'an; said by al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you not transgress﴾. al-Zajjāj mentioned two possibilities for "an" (that). The first: it has the meaning of "li" (in order that); the meaning being: "so that you do not transgress." The second: it is explanatory, so "lā" is for prohibition; the meaning being: "that is, do not transgress," i.e., do not exceed justice. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not diminish the balance﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: that is, do not reduce the weight.

As for "al-anām" (the creatures), concerning them there are three opinions. The first: they are the people; narrated by ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās. The second: every living being; narrated by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās, and this was said by (p-108) Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, Qatāda, al-Suddī, and al-Farrāʾ. The third: humans and jinn; said by al-Ḥasan and al-Zajjāj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In it is fruit﴾, that is, what is enjoyed of the various kinds of fruits. ﴿And the palm tree with its sheaths﴾. The sheaths (al-akmām) are the containers and coverings. We have fully explained this in [Ḥā Mīm al-Sajda: 47].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the grain﴾, meaning: all grains, such as wheat, barley, and other things. Ibn ʿĀmir recited "wal-ḥabba" with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, "dhā al-ʿaṣfi" with an alif, and "wal-raiḥāna" with a fatḥa on the nūn. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī except Ibn Abī Surayj, and Khalaf recited "wal-ḥabbu dhū al-ʿaṣfi wal-rayḥāni" with a kasra on the nūn; the rest recited with a ḍamma on the nūn.

Concerning "al-ʿaṣf" there are two opinions. The first: it is the chaff of the crop and its leaves, which the winds scatter; said by Ibn ʿAbbās. Likewise Mujāhid said: it is the leaves of the crop. Ibn Qutayba said: al-ʿaṣf is the leaves of the crop, which then, when dry and withered and threshed, become chaff. The second: al-ʿaṣf is the part of the grain that is eaten; related by al-Farrāʾ.

Concerning "al-rayḥān" there are four opinions.

The first: it is sustenance; narrated by ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās, and this was said by Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddī. al-Farrāʾ said: "al-rayḥān" in the speech of the Arabs means sustenance; you say: "We went out seeking God's rayḥān." al-Zajjāj recited for al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

"The greeting of God, His rayḥān, His mercy, and rain-clouds pouring down."

(p-109) The second: it is the greenness of the crop; narrated by al-Wālibī from Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī said: on this view, it was called rayḥān because the soul rests by looking at it.

The third: it is your rayḥān which is smelled; al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "al-rayḥān" is what the earth produces of rayḥān (basil), and this is the view of al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: it is what is not eaten of the grain, while al-ʿaṣf is what is eaten of it; related by al-Farrāʾ.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ If it is asked: how is the address to two when He only mentioned man alone? Concerning this there are two answers, mentioned by al-Farrāʾ. The first: the Arabs address one person with the dual verb, as we explained in His saying: ﴿Cast into Hell﴾ [Qāf: 24]. The second: the reminder is meant to include man and jinn, so the address applies to both from the beginning of the sūra to its end. al-Zajjāj said: when God, exalted is He, mentioned in this sūra what indicates His oneness—the creation of man, the teaching of speech, the creation of the sun, moon, heaven, and earth—He addressed jinn and men, saying: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?" meaning: which of the blessings of your Lord from these mentioned things will you deny, for all of them are blessings bestowed upon you, in their indicating His oneness to you and in His providing you with sustenance by which your life is sustained. Ibn Qutayba said: al-ālāʾ are blessings; its singular is alan, like qafan, and ilan, like mi'an.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (*Zad al-Masir*) on Surah 55, verses 14–25:

Allah's words, ﴿He created man﴾, mean Adam, "from clay like pottery" (*salsal*). We have already discussed *salsal* and *jann* in [al-Hijr: 26–27]. As for His words, ﴿like pottery﴾ (*fakhkhar*), Abu 'Ubayda said: he was created from dry clay that was not fired, so it makes a sound when struck, and because of its dryness it is like *fakhkhar*. *Fakhkhar* is that which has been fired in the fire.

As for *marij*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the tongue of fire that appears at its edge when it blazes. Mujahid said: it is the flame mixed, some of it with other parts, of red, yellow and green flame that rises over a fire when it is kindled. Muqatil said: it is the pure flame of fire without smoke. Abu 'Ubayda said: *marij* is a mixture of fire. Ibn Qutayba said: *marij* is the flame of fire, from your saying, "The thing *maraja*," when it became agitated and did not settle. al-Zajjaj said: it is the flame mixed with the blackness of fire.

If it is said: Allah has described the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, with different expressions. Sometimes He says, ﴿He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]; sometimes, ﴿from clay like pottery﴾; sometimes, ﴿from sticky clay﴾ [al-Saffat: 11]; sometimes, ﴿like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman: 14]; and sometimes, ﴿from black, moulded clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. The answer is: the origin was dust, which became clay; then it became like moulded black mud; then it became dry clay like pottery. These are reports about the states of his origin.

If it is said: what is the benefit of repeating His words, ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ The answer is that this repetition is to establish the blessings and to emphasise the reminder of them. Ibn Qutayba said: among the methods of the Arabs is repetition for emphasis and clarity, just as among their methods is brevity for lightness and conciseness, because the speaker's or orator's varying of his discourse in various arts is better than his limiting himself to one art in the same context. One of them says: "By God, I will not do it," then, "By God, I will not do it," when he wants to emphasise and cut off the hopes that he will do it. Like one who says, "By God, I will do it," omitting the "not" when he wants brevity. The hurried speaker says, "Hurry, hurry!" and to the archer, "Shoot, shoot!" The poet said:

"How many a blessing was his, and how many, and how many!"

Another said:

"Why did you not ask the hosts of Kinda on the day they turned their backs, 'Where? Where?'"

Sometimes an attribute comes and they want to emphasise it, but they dislike repeating it a second time, since it is a single word. So they change one letter of it and then attach it to the first, as in their saying: *'aṭshān naṭshān* (very thirsty), *shayṭān layṭān* (devil), *ḥasan basan* (very good). Ibn Durayd said: from *ittibā'* (echo-formation) are: *jā'iʿ nā'iʿ* (very hungry), *malīḥ qarīḥ* (very handsome), *qabīḥ shaqīḥ* (very ugly), *shaḥīḥ naḥīḥ* (very stingy), *khabīth nabīth* (very wicked), *kathīr babīr* (very much), *sayyigh layyigh* (smooth), *sā'igh lā'igh* (palatable), *ḥaqīr naqīr* (very small), *ḍa'īl ba'īl* (very thin), *khaḍir maḍir* (green), *'ifrīt nifrīt* (demon), *thiqa niqa* (trustworthy), *kinn inn* (wrap), *wāḥid fāḥid* (one), *ḥā'ir bā'ir* (bewildered), *samḥ lamḥ* (generous). Ibn Qutayba said: when Allah, Exalted, counted His bounties in this surah and reminded His servants of His favours, and alerted them to His power, He made each phrase of this kind a separator between every two blessings, so that He would make them understand the blessings and establish them in their minds, just as you say to a man: "Did I not settle you in a dwelling when you were homeless? Will you deny this? Did I not perform the pilgrimage on your behalf when you had never performed it? Will you deny this?"

Al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah narrated in his *Sahih* (a collection of authentic hadith) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Surah al-Rahman to us until he finished it. Then he said: 'Why do I see you silent? The jinn were better in their response than you. Every time I recited to them this verse, *So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?*, they said: "Nothing of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny. To You be praise."'"

Allah's words, ﴿Lord of the two easts﴾: Abu Raja' and Ibn Abi 'Abla read *rabbi l-mashriqayni wa rabbi l-maghribayn* with the genitive (*khafḍ*). They are the eastern point of summer and the eastern point of winter, and the western point of summer and the western point of winter, for the sun and the moon together.

Allah's words, ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾: that is, He sent forth the sweet and the salty and left them free, and made them ﴿meet﴾, ﴿between them is a barrier﴾, that is, a partition from the power of Allah, Exalted, ﴿they do not transgress﴾, that is, they do not mix, so that one does not transgress upon the other. Ibn 'Abbas said: the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth meet every year. al-Hasan said: ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾ means the sea of Persia and the sea of Rome; ﴿between them is a barrier﴾ means the islands. This has already been explained in [al-Furqan: 53].

Allah's words, ﴿From them emerge pearls and coral﴾: al-Zajjaj said: it emerges only from the salty sea, and He mentioned both because if it emerges from one of them, it has emerged from both. A similar usage is ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16]. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: He meant, "It emerges from one of them," and the qualifier was omitted. Ibn Jarir said: He said "from them" because it emerges from the shells of the sea by the drop of the sky.

As for pearls and coral, there are two opinions. One is that coral is what is small of pearls, and pearls are the large ones. This was said by most scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Farra'. al-Zajjaj said: *lu'lu'* is a collective term for the seeds that come out of the sea, and *marjan* are its small ones. The second is that *lu'lu'* are the small ones and *marjan* the large ones. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: when the sky rains, the shells open their mouths, and whatever rain falls into them is a pearl. Ibn Jarir said: wherever a drop falls, it becomes a pearl. I read to our shaykh, Abu Mansur the linguist, who said: some people of the language mentioned that *marjan* is a foreign word arabicised. Abu Bakr, meaning Ibn Durayd, said: I have not heard of a derived verb from it, and it is worthy of being so. Ibn Mas'ud said: *marjan* is red beads. al-Zajjaj said: *marjan* is very white. Abu Ya'la related that *marjan* is a kind of pearl like branches.

Allah's words, ﴿And His are the ships﴾, meaning the vessels, ﴿the raised up﴾ (*al-munsha'at*). Mujahid said: it means those whose sails have been raised, as opposed to those whose sails have not been raised. Ibn Qutayba said: they are those that were brought into being (*unshi'na*), that is, begun in the sea. Hamza read *al-munshi'at*, making them those that begin, as one says, "The cloud *anshaa'at*, rains," when it starts. The poet said... and *al-a'lam* are the mountains, and this has already been mentioned in [al-Shura: 32].

As for His words, ﴿like pottery﴾ (*fakhkhar*), Abu 'Ubayda said: he was created from dry clay that was not fired, so it makes a sound when struck, and because of its dryness it is like *fakhkhar*. *Fakhkhar* is that which has been fired in the fire.

As for *marij*, Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the tongue of fire that appears at its edge when it blazes. Mujahid said: it is the flame mixed, some of it with other parts, of red, yellow and green flame that rises over a fire when it is kindled. Muqatil said: it is the pure flame of fire without smoke. Abu 'Ubayda said: *marij* is a mixture of fire. Ibn Qutayba said: *marij* is the flame of fire, from your saying, "The thing *maraja*," when it became agitated and did not settle. al-Zajjaj said: it is the flame mixed with the blackness of fire.

If it is said: Allah has described the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, with different expressions. Sometimes He says, ﴿He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]; sometimes, ﴿from clay like pottery﴾; sometimes, ﴿from sticky clay﴾ [al-Saffat: 11]; sometimes, ﴿like pottery﴾ [al-Rahman: 14]; and sometimes, ﴿from black, moulded clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. The answer is: the origin was dust, which became clay; then it became like moulded black mud; then it became dry clay like pottery. These are reports about the states of his origin.

If it is said: what is the benefit of repeating His words, ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ The answer is that this repetition is to establish the blessings and to emphasise the reminder of them. Ibn Qutayba said: among the methods of the Arabs is repetition for emphasis and clarity, just as among their methods is brevity for lightness and conciseness, because the speaker's or orator's varying of his discourse in various arts is better than his limiting himself to one art in the same context. One of them says: "By God, I will not do it," then, "By God, I will not do it," when he wants to emphasise and cut off the hopes that he will do it. Like one who says, "By God, I will do it," omitting the "not" when he wants brevity. The hurried speaker says, "Hurry, hurry!" and to the archer, "Shoot, shoot!" The poet said:

"How many a blessing was his, and how many, and how many!"

Another said:

"Why did you not ask the hosts of Kinda on the day they turned their backs, 'Where? Where?'"

Sometimes an attribute comes and they want to emphasise it, but they dislike repeating it a second time, since it is a single word. So they change one letter of it and then attach it to the first, as in their saying: *'aṭshān naṭshān* (very thirsty), *shayṭān layṭān* (devil), *ḥasan basan* (very good). Ibn Durayd said: from *ittibā'* (echo-formation) are: *jā'iʿ nā'iʿ* (very hungry), *malīḥ qarīḥ* (very handsome), *qabīḥ shaqīḥ* (very ugly), *shaḥīḥ naḥīḥ* (very stingy), *khabīth nabīth* (very wicked), *kathīr babīr* (very much), *sayyigh layyigh* (smooth), *sā'igh lā'igh* (palatable), *ḥaqīr naqīr* (very small), *ḍa'īl ba'īl* (very thin), *khaḍir maḍir* (green), *'ifrīt nifrīt* (demon), *thiqa niqa* (trustworthy), *kinn inn* (wrap), *wāḥid fāḥid* (one), *ḥā'ir bā'ir* (bewildered), *samḥ lamḥ* (generous). Ibn Qutayba said: when Allah, Exalted, counted His bounties in this surah and reminded His servants of His favours, and alerted them to His power, He made each phrase of this kind a separator between every two blessings, so that He would make them understand the blessings and establish them in their minds, just as you say to a man: "Did I not settle you in a dwelling when you were homeless? Will you deny this? Did I not perform the pilgrimage on your behalf when you had never performed it? Will you deny this?"

Al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah narrated in his *Sahih* (a collection of authentic hadith) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Surah al-Rahman to us until he finished it. Then he said: 'Why do I see you silent? The jinn were better in their response than you. Every time I recited to them this verse, *So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?*, they said: "Nothing of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny. To You be praise."'"

Allah's words, ﴿Lord of the two easts﴾: Abu Raja' and Ibn Abi 'Abla read *rabbi l-mashriqayni wa rabbi l-maghribayn* with the genitive (*khafḍ*). They are the eastern point of summer and the eastern point of winter, and the western point of summer and the western point of winter, for the sun and the moon together.

Allah's words, ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾: that is, He sent forth the sweet and the salty and left them free, and made them ﴿meet﴾, ﴿between them is a barrier﴾, that is, a partition from the power of Allah, Exalted, ﴿they do not transgress﴾, that is, they do not mix, so that one does not transgress upon the other. Ibn 'Abbas said: the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth meet every year. al-Hasan said: ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾ means the sea of Persia and the sea of Rome; ﴿between them is a barrier﴾ means the islands. This has already been explained in [al-Furqan: 53].

Allah's words, ﴿From them emerge pearls and coral﴾: al-Zajjaj said: it emerges only from the salty sea, and He mentioned both because if it emerges from one of them, it has emerged from both. A similar usage is ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16]. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: He meant, "It emerges from one of them," and the qualifier was omitted. Ibn Jarir said: He said "from them" because it emerges from the shells of the sea by the drop of the sky.

As for pearls and coral, there are two opinions. One is that coral is what is small of pearls, and pearls are the large ones. This was said by most scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Farra'. al-Zajjaj said: *lu'lu'* is a collective term for the seeds that come out of the sea, and *marjan* are its small ones. The second is that *lu'lu'* are the small ones and *marjan* the large ones. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: when the sky rains, the shells open their mouths, and whatever rain falls into them is a pearl. Ibn Jarir said: wherever a drop falls, it becomes a pearl. I read to our shaykh, Abu Mansur the linguist, who said: some people of the language mentioned that *marjan* is a foreign word arabicised. Abu Bakr, meaning Ibn Durayd, said: I have not heard of a derived verb from it, and it is worthy of being so. Ibn Mas'ud said: *marjan* is red beads. al-Zajjaj said: *marjan* is very white. Abu Ya'la related that *marjan* is a kind of pearl like branches.

Allah's words, ﴿And His are the ships﴾, meaning the vessels, ﴿the raised up﴾ (*al-munsha'at*). Mujahid said: it means those whose sails have been raised, as opposed to those whose sails have not been raised. Ibn Qutayba said: they are those that were brought into being (*unshi'na*), that is, begun in the sea. Hamza read *al-munshi'at*, making them those that begin, as one says, "The cloud *anshaa'at*, rains," when it starts. The poet said... and *al-a'lam* are the mountains, and this has already been mentioned in [al-Shura: 32].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 55, verse 26–30:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾. That is, upon the earth. It is a metaphor for what is not mentioned. "Fani" (perishing): that is, destroyed.

﴿And there will remain the Face of your Lord﴾. That is, your Lord will remain, ﴿Full of Majesty and Honor﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: "Al-jalal" (majesty) is the verbal noun of "jalil" (the Majestic); it is said: "jalil bayyin al-jalala wa'l-jalal" (one who is clearly majestic). "Al-ikram" (honor) is the verbal noun of "akrama, yukrimu, ikraman." The meaning is that God, the Exalted, deserves to be magnified and honored, and not to be denied or disbelieved in. It may also be understood to mean that He honors the people of His friendship and raises their ranks. It may also be that one of the two matters, namely "al-jalal," is attributed to God, the Exalted, in the sense of an attribute of His, while the other, namely "al-ikram," is attributed to the servant in the sense of an action from him, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He is worthy of piety and worthy of forgiveness﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 56], so one of the two matters refers to God, which is forgiveness, and the other refers to the servants, which is piety.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾. The meaning is that all of them are in need of Him, so they ask Him, while He is free of need from them. ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾, such as giving life and causing death, granting might and bringing humiliation, curing the sick, giving to the one who asks, and other of His acts. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is the driving of decrees toward their appointed times. Muqatil said: the occasion of the revelation of this verse was that the Jews said: "God does not decide anything on the Sabbath day," so this verse was revealed: ﴿"Every day He is in a matter."﴾

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (*Zad al-Masir*) on Surah 55, verses 37–45:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then when the sky splits apart﴾, meaning: it is cleft from the Milky Way (*al-Majarra*) for the descent of those in it on the Day of Resurrection. "And it becomes red like a rose (*wardah*)," and concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: it is like the color of a rose-colored horse (*al-faras al-wardah*). This was said by Abu Salih and al-Dahhak. Al-Farra' said: the rose-colored horse (*al-faras al-wardah*) is, in spring, rose-colored tending toward yellow; when the heat intensifies, it becomes a deep red rose; and after that it becomes a rose tending toward dust-color (*al-ghubrah*). So he likened the sky's changing colors to the changing of the rose-colored horse's coat. Likewise al-Zajjaj said: "*fa-kanat wardah*" means: like the color of a rose-colored horse. And al-Kumayt (said): the *warad* change color, so their color in winter differs from their color in summer, and their color in summer differs from their color in winter. Thus the sky changes color from the Great Terror. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: it became red, in the color of the rose-colored horse.

The second: it is the rose of plants (*wardat al-nabat*), whose colors vary, though redness predominates over them. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Concerning *al-dihan* (﴿كَالدِّهَانِ﴾, "like oil/molten dregs" in the verse) there are two opinions. The first: it is singular, namely the red leather (*al-adim al-ahmar*), said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is the plural of *duhn* (oil), and oil varies in color between green, red and yellow. This was related by al-Yazidi, and Mujahid went to a similar view. Al-Farra' said: He likened the sky's changing color to the changing of the rose-colored horse's coat, and likened the rose in the variety of its colors to *al-dihan*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So on that Day, neither man nor jinn will be asked about his sin﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: they will not be asked so that their state may be known, because Allah, exalted is He, knows them better than they know themselves.

The second: none of them will ask another about his condition, because each is occupied with himself. Both views were related from Ibn Abbas.

The third: they will not be asked about their sins, because they are recognized by their marks (*simah*): the disbeliever has a blackened face, and the believer has a bright face and white marks (*aghurr muhajjal*) from the traces of his ablution. This was said by al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: no one will be asked about his sin in order to inquire, but he will be asked a question of reproach (*su'al tawbikh*).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾. Al-Hasan said: by the blackness of their faces and the blueness of their eyes. ﴿So they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: the guardians of Hell (*khazanat Jahannam*) gather their forelocks to their feet from behind their backs, then thrust them on their faces into the Fire. This was said by Muqatil. The second: they are seized by the forelocks and the feet, and then dragged into the Fire. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Murdawayh al-Sa'igh related that he said: The imam led us in the dawn prayer and recited Surah "al-Rahman," and with us was Ali ibn al-Fudayl ibn Iyad. When he recited ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾, Ali fell unconscious until we had finished the prayer. Afterwards we said to him: Did you not hear the imam recite ﴿Maqsuratun fi al-khiyam (chaste, cloistered ones in pavilions)﴾? He said: That occupied me from it: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks, so they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is Hell﴾, meaning: it will be said to them, "This is Hell ﴿which the criminals used to deny﴾," meaning the polytheists. ﴿They will go around between it and﴾ — Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read *yutawwifun* with a damma on the *ya'* and a shadda on the *waw*; al-A'mash read the same, except with a *ta'* (*yuttawwifun*).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and between scalding water (*hamim an*)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-hamim* is hot water, and *al-ani* is that whose intensity of heat has reached its limit. The exegetes said: the meaning is that they will run between the torment of the blazing Fire and the *hamim*; when they seek relief from the Fire, their relief will be made to be the scalding water of intense heat.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 55, verses 46–53:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But for one who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. There are two opinions regarding this.

The first: his standing before his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Recompense.

The second: God's standing over His servant, reckoning what he has earned.

It is mentioned in the tafsir (the exegetical literature on the Qur'an), that the servant intends a sin and then abandons it out of fear of God, Mighty and Majestic (p-120), so he has two gardens, and they are two orchards.

﴿Possessing branches﴾. There are two opinions regarding this.

The first: that they are the branches, plural of fanan, which is the straight branch in length. This is the opinion of Mujahid, Ikrimah, Ata', al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj.

The second: that they are the varieties and kinds of everything, plural of fann. This is the opinion of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Dahhak said: possessing varieties of fruit.

Ata' combined the two opinions and said: on every branch are varieties of fruit.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In them are two flowing springs﴾. Ibn Abbas said: they flow with pure water, one of them is Salsabil, and the other is Tasnim. Ata' said: one of them is of water that does not spoil, and the other is of wine. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "In them are two flowing springs" is for the one who had, in the world, two eyes flowing with weeping.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In them are two of every fruit, a pair﴾. That is, two kinds and two types. The exegetes said: in them are two types of everything with which one enjoys fruit, fresh and dry, neither of which is inferior to the other in excellence.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 55, verses 54–61:**

﴿Reclining﴾: this describes those mentioned, ﴿on couches﴾, the plural of *firash* (couch). ﴿Whose linings﴾ are the plural of *bitana* (lining), which is the part beneath the outer surface (*zihara*).

Abu Hurayra said: "These are the linings, so what do you think of the outer surfaces?!" Ibn Abbas said: "Only the description of the outer surfaces was omitted, because no one knows what they are." Qatada said: "The linings are the outer surfaces in the dialect of a people." Al-Farra' used to say: "The lining may be the outer surface, and the outer surface may be the lining, since each of the two may be a face. The Arabs say: 'This is the back (*zahr*) of the sky' and 'this is the belly (*batn*) of the sky,' referring to its outer side, which is what we see." Ibn al-Zubayr, criticizing the killers of Uthman, said: "They came out against him like thieves from behind the village, so God killed them in every way, and those among them who escaped did so beneath the bellies of the stars." He meant that they fled at night, so they made the backs of the stars into bellies, and that is permissible in Arabic. Ibn Qutayba strongly rejected this view and said: "God intended to make us understand, in a way we can grasp, the excellence of these couches, and that what lies on the earth side of them is brocade. If the lining is like that, then the outer surface is higher and more noble. Would it be permissible for someone to say of the face of a worshipper, 'This is his lining,' and of the side facing the ground, 'This is his outer surface'? This usage is only permissible for something with two equal faces. You say of the side of a wall facing you, 'This is the back of the wall,' and your neighbor says of the side facing him, 'This is the back of the wall.' Likewise, the side of the sky facing us is its back, while for those above it, it is its belly."

We have already mentioned *istabraq* (brocade) in [the commentary on] Surah al-Kahf (18:31). Regarding God's words ﴿and the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾, Abu Ubayda said: that is, what is picked is near, and does not tire the one who picks it.

God's words ﴿therein are those restraining their gaze﴾: we have explained this in Surah al-Saffat (37:48).

Regarding His words ﴿therein﴾, there are two views:

One is that it refers to the two gardens and other things prepared for the person addressed in this account, as stated by al-Zajjaj. The second is that it refers to the couches, as mentioned by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

God's words ﴿untouched by man or jinn before them﴾: al-Kisa'i read *yatmithhunna* with a *damma* on the *mim* (*yatmuthhunna*), while the rest read it with a *kasra* (*yatmithhunna*). Both are dialectal forms, like *ya'kifu* and *ya'kufu*. There are two views on its meaning:

One: they have not deflowered them. *Tamth* means intercourse involving the breaking of the hymen, and from this comes the term *tamith* for a menstruating woman. This was stated by al-Farra'.

The second: they have not touched them. It is said: "No camel-mare was ever mounted (*ma tamatha hadha al-ba'ir habl*)," meaning no one touched it. This was stated by Abu Ubayda. Muqatil said: "This is because they were created from Paradise; according to his view, this is a description of the houris." Al-Sha'bi said: "They are from the women of this world, whom no one has touched since they were created." The verse is evidence that a jinn can have intercourse with a woman just as a human can.

God's words ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾: Qatada said: "They are in the clarity of rubies and the whiteness of coral." Al-Zajjaj mentioned that the scholars of tafsir and of language said: "They are in the clarity of rubies and the whiteness of coral, and coral is small pearls, which are even whiter." *of emerald, ruby and gold."*

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 55, verse 62–78:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And besides these two there are two other gardens﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: for the one who fears the standing before his Lord there are two gardens, and besides these two he has two other gardens.

Regarding His saying ﴿besides these two﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: "besides them" in rank, as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: "besides them" in excellence, as Abu Musa reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Two gardens of gold, and two gardens of silver." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil followed this view.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿dark green﴾. Ibn Abbas [and Ibn al-Zubayr] said: green from the abundance of water. Abu Ubayda said: from their greenness they have become black. Al-Zajjaj said: It means that they are green, their greenness inclining towards blackness, and every green plant reaches the completion of its greenness and its watering when it inclines towards blackness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿two gushing springs﴾. Abu Ubayda said: two gushing (fawwaratan). Ibn Qutayba said: two flowing (tafurran), and "al-nadkh" (gushing) is more intense than "al-nadh" (sprinkling). Concerning what they gush forth with, there are four opinions.

The first: with musk and camphor, said by Ibn Masud. The second: with water, said by Ibn Abbas. The third: with goodness and blessing, said by al-Hasan. The fourth: with varieties of fruit, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and date palms and pomegranates﴾. Ibn Abbas said: The date palms of Paradise: their trunks are of green emerald, their spathes (kerab) are of red gold, and their fronds are the clothing of the people of Paradise, from which are their cut garments and their robes. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The date palms of Paradise: their trunks are of gold, their roots are of gold, their stalks (karanif) are of emerald, and their dates are like buckets, whiter than milk, softer than butter, sweeter than honey, with no stone in them. Abu Ubayda said: al-karanif are the thick bases of the fronds; the singular is karnafa. The mention of the date palm and the pomegranate again, though they have already entered under fruit, is to show their excellence, as we mentioned in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]. This is the view of the majority of exegetes and linguists. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj related that some people said: they are not of the fruit. Al-Farra' said: They have taken a position, but the Arabs do count them as fruit. Al-Azhari said: I know of no Arab who said about palm trees and vines and their produce that they are not of the fruit; rather, whoever said so did so out of little knowledge of Arabic speech. The Arabs mention things in general and then single out some of them by name to draw attention to their excellence, as in His saying: ﴿and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]. Whoever said that they are not of the angels has disbelieved, and whoever said that the fruit of the date palm and pomegranate are not of the fruit has erred.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿therein﴾, meaning in the four gardens, are ﴿good [women]﴾, meaning the houris. Mu'adh al-Qari, Asim al-Jahdari and Abu Nuhayk read "khayyirat" with a shadda on the ya'. The linguists said: the original is "khayyirat" with the shadda, which was lightened, as it is said "hayn layn" and "hayyin layyin". Umm Salama related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of characters, the fairest of faces."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿chaste, secluded in their pavilions [houris]﴾. We have explained the meaning of the houris in Surah al-Dukhan [44:54].

Regarding "maqsurat" (secluded) there are two opinions.

The first: those confined within the tents (hijal), said by Ibn Abbas; this is the view of al-Hasan, Abu al-Aliya, al-Qurazi, al-Dahhak and Abu Salih.

The second: those who restrict their gaze to their husbands, so they do not raise their eyes to others, said by al-Rabi'. Mujahid is reported to have held both views. The first is more sound, for the Arabs say: "imra'a maqsura", "qasira" and "qasura" when a woman remains constant in her seclusion. Kuthayyir said:

"By my life, you have made every short woman beloved to me, though the short women do not know of that.
I meant the short women of the tents, and did not mean the short-stepped, the worst of women, the squat ones."

Some recite it as "qasura" and "qasuruat"; and "al-bahatir" means the short ones.

Regarding "al-khiyam" (pavilions) there are two opinions.

The first: that they are houses.

The second: tents attached to palaces. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs related from the hadith of Abu Musa from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, for the believer in Paradise there is a tent of a single hollow pearl, its height in the sky sixty miles; the believer has families in it, and he goes around to them, and they do not see one another." Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas said: The khiyam are hollow pearls. Ibn Abbas said: The tent is a single pearl, four farsakh by four farsakh, having four thousand doors of gold.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿reclining on green cushions﴾. Uthman ibn Affan, Asim al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read "ʿala rafaraf" as a non-diptote plural. Al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliya and Abu Imran al-Jawni read the same, except that they declined "rafarif". Tha'lab said: He did not say "akhdar" (singular) because rafraf is a plural whose singular is rafrafa, as in His saying: ﴿who has made for you from the green tree fire﴾ [Ya Sin: 80], and He did not say "khudr", because shajar is a plural; you say: "hadha hasan abyad" and "hasan aswad". The poet said:

"Truly, servants of God, I am not walking with Hirjab as long as the arak tree is green (khudr) there."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of ar-rafraf in three opinions.

The first: that they are the excess of the cushions and carpets, related by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. Abu Ubayda said: they are the mattresses and rugs. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba related that they are the cushions. Al-Naqqash said: The rafraf are the green cushions above the mattresses.

The second: that they are the gardens of Paradise, related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise.

The third: that they are the pillows, said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and beautiful carpets﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions.

The first: that they are the rugs (zarabi), said by Ibn Abbas, Ata', Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd; and Ibn Qutayba likewise said: al-'abqari is the thick cushions. Abu Ubayda said: Every kind of rug is called 'abqari.

The second: that it is thick brocade, said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: The original meaning of 'abqari in the language is an adjective for anything described with exaggeration; its origin is that 'Abqar was a land where rugs and other things were woven, so every excellent thing was attributed to it. Zuhayr said:

"With horses upon which is a jinn of 'abqar, deserving that one day they attain and rise above."

Uthman ibn Affan, Asim al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read "wa-'abaqiri" with an alif, the qaf kasra, the ya fathah, without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: This reading has no basis in Arabic, because the plural after its alif has two letters, like masajid and mafatih, and it cannot take the form of 'abaqiri, since what exceeds three letters is not pluralized with the ya of nisba. If you pluralized "'abqari" it would be "abaqira", just as the plural of "muhlibi" is "mahaliba", and you would not say "mahalibi". He said: If it is said that "'abqari" is singular and "hisan" is plural, how is this permissible? The answer: the singular of this is "'abqariyya" and the plural is "'abqari", as you say: tamra and tamr, lawza and lawz; and "'abqari" may also be a noun of genus.

Al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliya and Abu Imran read "wa-'abaqari" with an alif and tanwin.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions.

The first: that the mention of "the name" is extra, and the meaning is: Blessed is your Lord.

The second: that it is original.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is: "tafa'ala" from blessing, that is, blessing is obtained and acquired by mentioning His name. We have explained the meaning of "tabaraka" in [al-A'raf: 54], and we mentioned the meaning of ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 27] in this surah. Ibn Amir used to read "dhu al-jalal", and so it is in the codices of the people of Syria; the rest read "dhi al-jalal", and so it is in the codices of the people of the Hijaz and Iraq, and they all agree on the first place that it is "dhu".

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is: "tafa'ala" from blessing, that is, blessing is obtained and acquired by mentioning His name. We have explained the meaning of "tabaraka" in [al-A'raf: 54], and we mentioned the meaning of ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 27] in this surah. Ibn Amir used to read "dhu al-jalal", and so it is in the codices of the people of Syria; the rest read "dhi al-jalal", and so it is in the codices of the people of the Hijaz and Iraq, and they all agree on the first place that it is "dhu".

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 55, verse 62–78:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And besides these two there are two other gardens﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: for the one who fears the standing before his Lord there are two gardens, and besides these two he has two other gardens.

Regarding His saying ﴿besides these two﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: "besides them" in rank, as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: "besides them" in excellence, as Abu Musa reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Two gardens of gold, and two gardens of silver." Ibn Zayd and Muqatil followed this view.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿dark green﴾. Ibn Abbas [and Ibn al-Zubayr] said: green from the abundance of water. Abu Ubayda said: from their greenness they have become black. Al-Zajjaj said: It means that they are green, their greenness inclining towards blackness, and every green plant reaches the completion of its greenness and its watering when it inclines towards blackness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿two gushing springs﴾. Abu Ubayda said: two gushing (fawwaratan). Ibn Qutayba said: two flowing (tafurran), and "al-nadkh" (gushing) is more intense than "al-nadh" (sprinkling). Concerning what they gush forth with, there are four opinions.

The first: with musk and camphor, said by Ibn Masud. The second: with water, said by Ibn Abbas. The third: with goodness and blessing, said by al-Hasan. The fourth: with varieties of fruit, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and date palms and pomegranates﴾. Ibn Abbas said: The date palms of Paradise: their trunks are of green emerald, their spathes (kerab) are of red gold, and their fronds are the clothing of the people of Paradise, from which are their cut garments and their robes. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The date palms of Paradise: their trunks are of gold, their roots are of gold, their stalks (karanif) are of emerald, and their dates are like buckets, whiter than milk, softer than butter, sweeter than honey, with no stone in them. Abu Ubayda said: al-karanif are the thick bases of the fronds; the singular is karnafa. The mention of the date palm and the pomegranate again, though they have already entered under fruit, is to show their excellence, as we mentioned in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]. This is the view of the majority of exegetes and linguists. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj related that some people said: they are not of the fruit. Al-Farra' said: They have taken a position, but the Arabs do count them as fruit. Al-Azhari said: I know of no Arab who said about palm trees and vines and their produce that they are not of the fruit; rather, whoever said so did so out of little knowledge of Arabic speech. The Arabs mention things in general and then single out some of them by name to draw attention to their excellence, as in His saying: ﴿and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]. Whoever said that they are not of the angels has disbelieved, and whoever said that the fruit of the date palm and pomegranate are not of the fruit has erred.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿therein﴾, meaning in the four gardens, are ﴿good [women]﴾, meaning the houris. Mu'adh al-Qari, Asim al-Jahdari and Abu Nuhayk read "khayyirat" with a shadda on the ya'. The linguists said: the original is "khayyirat" with the shadda, which was lightened, as it is said "hayn layn" and "hayyin layyin". Umm Salama related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best of characters, the fairest of faces."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿chaste, secluded in their pavilions [houris]﴾. We have explained the meaning of the houris in Surah al-Dukhan [44:54].

Regarding "maqsurat" (secluded) there are two opinions.

The first: those confined within the tents (hijal), said by Ibn Abbas; this is the view of al-Hasan, Abu al-Aliya, al-Qurazi, al-Dahhak and Abu Salih.

The second: those who restrict their gaze to their husbands, so they do not raise their eyes to others, said by al-Rabi'. Mujahid is reported to have held both views. The first is more sound, for the Arabs say: "imra'a maqsura", "qasira" and "qasura" when a woman remains constant in her seclusion. Kuthayyir said:

"By my life, you have made every short woman beloved to me, though the short women do not know of that.
I meant the short women of the tents, and did not mean the short-stepped, the worst of women, the squat ones."

Some recite it as "qasura" and "qasuruat"; and "al-bahatir" means the short ones.

Regarding "al-khiyam" (pavilions) there are two opinions.

The first: that they are houses.

The second: tents attached to palaces. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs related from the hadith of Abu Musa from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, for the believer in Paradise there is a tent of a single hollow pearl, its height in the sky sixty miles; the believer has families in it, and he goes around to them, and they do not see one another." Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas said: The khiyam are hollow pearls. Ibn Abbas said: The tent is a single pearl, four farsakh by four farsakh, having four thousand doors of gold.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿reclining on green cushions﴾. Uthman ibn Affan, Asim al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read "ʿala rafaraf" as a non-diptote plural. Al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliya and Abu Imran al-Jawni read the same, except that they declined "rafarif". Tha'lab said: He did not say "akhdar" (singular) because rafraf is a plural whose singular is rafrafa, as in His saying: ﴿who has made for you from the green tree fire﴾ [Ya Sin: 80], and He did not say "khudr", because shajar is a plural; you say: "hadha hasan abyad" and "hasan aswad". The poet said:

"Truly, servants of God, I am not walking with Hirjab as long as the arak tree is green (khudr) there."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of ar-rafraf in three opinions.

The first: that they are the excess of the cushions and carpets, related by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. Abu Ubayda said: they are the mattresses and rugs. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba related that they are the cushions. Al-Naqqash said: The rafraf are the green cushions above the mattresses.

The second: that they are the gardens of Paradise, related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise.

The third: that they are the pillows, said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and beautiful carpets﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions.

The first: that they are the rugs (zarabi), said by Ibn Abbas, Ata', Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd; and Ibn Qutayba likewise said: al-'abqari is the thick cushions. Abu Ubayda said: Every kind of rug is called 'abqari.

The second: that it is thick brocade, said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: The original meaning of 'abqari in the language is an adjective for anything described with exaggeration; its origin is that 'Abqar was a land where rugs and other things were woven, so every excellent thing was attributed to it. Zuhayr said:

"With horses upon which is a jinn of 'abqar, deserving that one day they attain and rise above."

Uthman ibn Affan, Asim al-Jahdari and Ibn Muhaysin read "wa-'abaqiri" with an alif, the qaf kasra, the ya fathah, without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: This reading has no basis in Arabic, because the plural after its alif has two letters, like masajid and mafatih, and it cannot take the form of 'abaqiri, since what exceeds three letters is not pluralized with the ya of nisba. If you pluralized "'abqari" it would be "abaqira", just as the plural of "muhlibi" is "mahaliba", and you would not say "mahalibi". He said: If it is said that "'abqari" is singular and "hisan" is plural, how is this permissible? The answer: the singular of this is "'abqariyya" and the plural is "'abqari", as you say: tamra and tamr, lawza and lawz; and "'abqari" may also be a noun of genus.

Al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliya and Abu Imran read "wa-'abaqari" with an alif and tanwin.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions.

The first: that the mention of "the name" is extra, and the meaning is: Blessed is your Lord.

The second: that it is original.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is: "tafa'ala" from blessing, that is, blessing is obtained and acquired by mentioning His name. We have explained the meaning of "tabaraka" in [al-A'raf: 54], and we mentioned the meaning of ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 27] in this surah. Ibn Amir used to read "dhu al-jalal", and so it is in the codices of the people of Syria; the rest read "dhi al-jalal", and so it is in the codices of the people of the Hijaz and Iraq, and they all agree on the first place that it is "dhu".
